title: Chapter 68: A Thing Put Back, Part 3 of 5: Hard Words
html:
The hard word was CLOTH.
It came in the fifth line. NOT THROUGH CLOTH. And THROUGH had nearly killed her already. She had sat with her finger on it for so long that the brazier had burned down and Doctor Silas had got up, without a word, and fed it more coal from the sack, and sat down again. T. H. R. O. U. G. H. It did not sound like anything. It did not sound like its letters at all. Tuh-huh-ruh-oh-uh-guh-huh. She said it under her breath six times and it was still nonsense.
Then Mrs. Doyle, behind her, said very softly, "Not through cloth, love. Like a needle. Through."
And Juno saw it. All at once. Through. Like through a door. Of course.
She was angry for a moment. Then she was not, because Mrs. Doyle could only read her own name, Juno knew, and so she had not read it, she had guessed it, the way you guess the end of a song. And she had guessed right.
"Through," said Juno. "Not through cloth."
And then CLOTH. C. L. O. T. H. Another TH. She glared at it.
Doctor Silas leaned forward on his stool.
"Shall I..." he said gently. He held out one long red hand, palm up, toward the paper. "I could read it through once, quickly, and then you could..."
"No," said Juno.
It came out sharper than she meant. She saw him blink behind his crooked spectacles.
"No," she said again, more quietly. "Thank you, Doctor. But no." She put her finger on the bottom of the page, on the two small lines at the very end. "He wrote READ IT SLOW. To me. With my name. He didn't write let the doctor read it. He wrote Juno, read it slow." She looked up at Silas. "So I'm reading it slow."
Silas looked at her for a long moment.
Then he took his hand back, and folded his long arms round his long knees, and nodded. And something came into his tired gray face that Juno had not seen there before. She thought it might have been respect. Or it might have been the heat of the brazier.
"Quite right," he said. "I beg your pardon."
She looked back at the page.
C. L. O. T. H.
"Cloth," she said. Because it had to be. Not through cloth. What else could it be?
She went on.
The morning went on with her. Juno knew it did, though there was no window in the crypt and no light but the brazier and the lamp and the candle by the sleeping children. She knew because Mrs. Doyle went up the stair twice, and came down again, and the second time she said the bell had gone for the fifth hour of the morning. She knew because the coal sack went down. She knew because her own neck ached from bending over the paper, and her eyes ached from the orange light, and her finger had a gray smear on the end of it from the pencil.
But she did not stop.
Some lines were easy. SAY THEIR NAME. She knew SAY, she knew THEIR, she knew NAME. That line she read straight off, in one breath, and felt a rush of something hot and fierce go up through her chest, like the feeling of jumping a gap between two roofs and landing on the other side.
Some lines were walls. OFFERING was a wall. BREATHE was a wall, with that E on the end that did nothing, that just sat there. She hated it. She sounded it every way she could think of. Breeth-ee. Brath-ee. Breath. Then Gideon, who had not said a word all morning, said flatly, without looking up, "Breathe. Like you breathe," and she saw it, and was angry, and was grateful, and said it.
"Breathe it toward them."
Gideon was sitting exactly as he had been. With his knees up. Watching her. Not the paper. Her. His flat gray eyes going back and forth, from her finger on the page to her mouth, from her mouth to her finger. As if he were reading it too, through her. Learning the shape of the words in her mouth.
And his hands, on his knees, had not stopped shaking.
They had been shaking since she held out the packet. Juno had seen it. Not much. A small fine tremble, all the time, like the hands of an old man. He did not seem to notice it. He did nothing to stop it. He sat with them on his knees and let them shake and looked at her mouth.
She did not say anything about it. She read.
And behind Gideon, against the wall, Big Gideon sat with his huge hands on his own knees, palms down, where his son had put them, and looked at the brazier, and did not blink, and did not hear a word.
Or Juno thought he did not.
Once, when she read the line about the name, the name you call them, she thought she saw the big broken-nosed face turn, a very little, toward the sound of her voice. Just a little. The way a sleeping dog's ear turns toward a door.
But when she looked again, it was looking at the brazier.
She went on.
It took her the rest of the morning. All of it. Line after line after line. And at the end of it she came down to the bottom of the page, to the long crowded lines where the letters ran together, and read them too, one word at a time, with her finger, and her lips moving. TELL. THE. BOY.
She stopped.
She looked at Gideon.
Then she read it. The whole line. Slowly. Every word.
"Tell the boy. Quick and warm. And it has to be something of his own. You can't put back what you don't give."
The crypt was silent.
And Juno put the paper down on her knee, very carefully, and sat back on her heels on the warm floor, and found that she was shaking almost as much as Gideon was, and that her face was wet, and that she did not care who saw.
What the Page Says
"Again," said Gideon.
Juno looked up.
"Again," said Gideon. "But not slow. Just what it says. In order. So I can hold it."
So she did. She did not read it this time. She did not need to. She had climbed every wall on that page, one by one, and now she knew the way. She looked at the paper to keep her place, and she said it in her own words, plain, in order, one thing after another, the way you tell someone the way to a house.
"You need a thing of your own," she said. "A memory. A real one. Not a story somebody told you. Something you were there for. And it has to be a warm one."
Gideon nodded. Once.
"If it's in a jar, you hold the jar in your bare hand. No glove. Till the glass is warm. As warm as your hand. If it's still in you, you put your hand on your own chest, here, till your hand's warm." She touched her own chest. "Warm first. It says that twice. Always warm first."
Gideon nodded.
"Then you sit with the one you're putting it into. Close. Skin to skin. Your hand on their hand, or their face. Somewhere bare. Not through cloth. Never through cloth."
She glanced, without meaning to, at Big Gideon's huge bare hands on his knees.
"Then you open the jar," said Juno. "Or you open your hand. And you breathe it toward them. Slow. Toward their face. Like breathing on a window to clear it. Not hard. It says you're not pushing. You're offering."
"Offering," said Gideon.
"And while you breathe, you say their name. Not the name on papers. The name you call them. The name you'd shout across a street." She swallowed. "And then you wait. It can take a long time. Sometimes it doesn't take at all. If it doesn't take, it wasn't warm enough. Or it wasn't yours."
The brazier ticked.
"And then the last bit," said Juno. "To you. Quick and warm, and it has to be something of your own. You can't put back what you don't give."
She stopped.
Nobody said anything for a long time.
Then Doctor Silas let out a long breath through his nose, and put his crooked spectacles back on, and rubbed his long face with both hands.
"That's all?" he said. Not to anyone. To the roof, perhaps. "That's all it is?"
"That's all it says," said Juno.
"Linus's book has four pages on it." Silas's voice was strange. "Four. I've read them a dozen times this week. Tables. Diagrams. The position of the hands. The phase of the moon, for Saints' sake. The proper words in the old letters. I couldn't make head or tail of it. I thought it must be beyond me. Beyond anyone." He laughed, very short, without any humor in it. "And it's this. Hold it till it's warm. Sit close. Breathe. Say their name."
Juno did not know what to say to that. She looked down at the page on her knee. It did not look clever. It looked like a tired man's big crooked letters, crowded together on a cut-out page, with two of them crossed out and done again. That was all.
It was enough, she thought. It had come all the way from the end of the world in a turnip cart, and it was enough.
"Maybe it only had to be simple," she said. "So somebody like me could read it."
Silas looked at her over his crooked spectacles for a long moment. Then he said, quietly, "Maybe it did," and did not say anything more.
Gideon had not moved. He was sitting with his knees up and his shaking hands on them, looking at the paper on Juno's knee.
"Something of your own," he said. Flat. "A thing you were there for. A warm one."
"Yes."
"I haven't got any warm ones."
He said it the way he said everything. Plainly. As if he were saying, it's raining, or the coal's run out.
"She took them," said Gideon. "The Lady. Four winters. Every Tuesday, in the cold room. All the warm ones first. Then the rest. I don't feel anything. I know things. I know that's my da." He did not look round at the big man against the wall. "I know I'm supposed to want him back. I know Saul's dead and I'm supposed to be sad. I know all that. But there's nothing warm in me to give him. It's all gone."
Juno did not know what to say.
Nobody did. Mrs. Doyle, behind her, made a small sound and put her red hand over her mouth.
"Not in you," said Doctor Silas quietly.
Gideon looked at him.
"Not in you, perhaps," said Silas. "But it doesn't say in you. Does it? It says, if it's in a jar." He was looking at Gideon very steadily over his crooked spectacles. "You had a jar, Gideon. When you came here. The harvester brought it out of the Lady's cellar for you. With your number on it."
The crypt went very still.
Gideon's face did not change. But his shaking hands came together on his knees, and gripped each other.
"H.297," he said.
The Choice
The jars were in a box under Doctor Silas's table.
It was an old wooden box that had once held candles, with CANDLES BEST TALLOW burned into the side of it, and a lid that did not fit. Gideon went and knelt by it and pulled it out into the orange light and lifted the lid off. Inside, in nests of straw, there were two small glass jars, the size of a big man's thumb, each one with a wax seal on top and a paper label tied round its neck with string.
He took them both out and held them in his two shaking hands.
One was cold. Juno could see it from where she sat. There was frost on it. A fine white fur of frost, all over the glass, that did not melt even in the heat of the crypt, and through the frost there was a faint gray light, like the light on a winter morning before the sun comes up.
"That's my cold," said Gideon. Flat. "From the Lady's cellar. The doctor says it's the first thing she took. The cold I had when I was little and couldn't stop shivering. The harvester brought it out with the other one." He put it back in the straw. "It's no good. It's not warm."
The other one he held up to the brazier.
It was not frosted. It was clear glass, a little greenish, with a lip round the neck and a plug of dark wax. Inside, very faint, there was a glow. Not gray. Gold. A soft warm gold, like a candle seen through a window on a winter night from a long way off. It moved a little, when the jar moved. As if it were alive.
The paper label round its neck had writing on it. In faded brown ink, very neat, in the Lady's clerk's hand. Juno could read it now.
H.297. GIDEON H. AGE 8. FIRST GLASS. THE DOCKS. HIS FATHER.
Gideon looked at it for a long time.
"What is it?" said Juno. "What's in it? Do you know?"
"The doctor told me." Gideon did not look away from the gold glow. "He read the label. And the harvester said, when he gave it me. He walked it, a bit. Just the edge. To see what it was." A pause. "It's my da carrying me. Down the docks. On his shoulders. When I was eight. The day he took me to see the big ships come in. The first time. It was summer and there were gulls and he was humming and I had my hands on his head." He said it all in the same flat voice, as if he were reading out a list of coal deliveries. "He couldn't sing. He couldn't hold a note. But he could hum. He was humming the tune. The carrying tune. The one I hum."
The crypt was very quiet.
"It's the best one," said Gideon. "The Lady said so. She said it was the warmest one she ever took off a child. She kept it for herself. She didn't sell it. She used to take it out and hold it, the harvester said, in the cold room, when she was sad."
Juno felt something go tight in her throat.
"Then," she said, slowly, working it out, "if you give it to him... If you put it into him..." She looked at the big man against the wall. "Then you won't have it."
Gideon looked at her.
"I haven't got it now," he said. "It's in a jar."
"But you'd never get it back. Ever. It says. You can't put back what you don't give. If you give it away, it's his. It's gone out of the jar and into him and you can never have it. Not ever. You'll never get to know what it was like. Your da carrying you. The gulls. Him humming." Her voice was cracking. She could not help it. "Gideon. It's the best one. She said. You'd never know."
Gideon looked down at the jar in his shaking hands. At the soft gold light moving inside it.
For a long moment he did not say anything.
Then he said, in exactly the same flat short voice as always:
"I don't feel it anyway."
He turned the jar, a little, in his fingers.
"I could hold it all day," he said. "I could open it and drink it and walk it till I was sick, the way the harvester does. And I wouldn't feel it. She took the feeling. All of it. Every Tuesday. I'd know it was warm. I'd know it was my da and the gulls and the humming. But it would be like reading about it on a wall." He did not look up. "It's no good to me."
Then he lifted his flat gray eyes and looked past Juno. Past Silas and Mrs. Doyle. At the big broken-nosed man sitting against the wall under the word DA, with his hands on his knees, looking at the fire.
"He would," said Gideon.
That was all he said.
He would.
Juno put her hands over her face.
When she took them away, Gideon was already getting up. Slowly. Carefully. On his feet with the two big toes missing, so that he walked a little stiffly, the way she did, on the sides. With the jar held in both his shaking hands against his chest. And he went across the warm floor of the crypt, past the brazier, past the fleet of little wooden boats, to the wall where his father sat.
And Doctor Silas stood up, and Mrs. Doyle stood up, and Juno stood up, and none of them went any nearer, and none of them said a word.
The Doing
Mrs. Doyle lit the candles.
Nobody asked her to. She put down her broom against a pillar and went to the basket she always kept at the foot of the stairs, and took out a bundle of the cheap tallow candles, and untied the string. And she went round the crypt with a taper from the brazier and lit them. One on the table. One on the box by the sleeping children. One on each pillar, stuck in its own grease on the old bricks. One on the floor by the brazier. One, two, three, all round, until the low arched roof was full of small yellow flames, and the shadows of the pillars went soft and many, and the orange glow of the brazier was a gold glow instead.
She put the last one on the floor beside Big Gideon. Close. Where its light fell on his face and his hands.
Then she went back to her broom and stood with it, and folded her red hands on top of it, and did not move again.
Gideon knelt down by his father.
The big man did not look at him. He went on looking at the brazier, past his son's shoulder. His huge scarred hands lay on his knees, palms down, the way Gideon had put them that morning, and every morning.
Gideon sat down. Not in front of him. Beside him. Against the wall. The way you sit beside someone on a step. His shoulder against his father's arm. His small thin body against the great heavy one. His legs out straight in front of him, like his father's. Side by side. The little feet in their boots beside the great feet in theirs.
And he took off his gloves.
He had cut-down gloves, knitted, gray, with holes in the fingers. He pulled them off with his teeth, one and then the other, and put them in his lap. His hands were small and pale and still shaking.
He took the jar in his bare right hand.
And held it.
Juno watched him. They all did. He sat there against the wall beside his father, with the little glass jar closed in his bare fist, and held it. Not tight. Just held it. The way you hold a bird you have caught, so that it cannot get away and cannot be hurt.
Warm first, the page said. Always warm first.
The candles burned. The brazier ticked. One of the children at the far end turned over in its sleep and murmured something.
Gideon held the jar.
It took a long time. The glass had been in a box under a table in a cold crypt for a long time. It was cold all the way through. Juno could see him feel it. She could see his small fingers tighten, a little, against the cold, and then loosen, and tighten. She saw him breathe on his own fist, once, the way you breathe on your hands in the snow, to help.
She counted. She could not help it. She counted the breaths. Lyra would have.
Sixty. Seventy. Eighty.
At a hundred and something, Gideon opened his fist and looked at the jar, and touched it to his cheek. Then closed his fist again.
A hundred and fifty.
And then he opened his hand, and the jar lay in his palm, and he looked at it, and nodded. Once. To himself.
Warm.
He turned to his father.
Skin to skin, the page said. Not through cloth. Never through cloth.
Gideon reached out with his left hand and took his father's right hand off his knee. It was so big that his own small hand could not close round it. It lay across his palm like a spade. Gray-brown and heavy, with the old white scars across the knuckles from the docks and the hooks. He held it in his lap. Then he slid his own hand down, so that his small palm lay flat against the big palm. Skin to skin.
The big man did not move. Did not look. Did not seem to know anything had happened at all.
Gideon lifted the jar.
He held it up, close, near his father's face. Near the broken nose and the hook-shaped scar. The candle on the floor beside them lit it from below, and the soft gold glow inside the glass shone up on both their faces, the big one and the small one, so that for a moment they looked alike. The same jaw. The same ears.
Gideon put his thumb on the wax.
It was soft, from the warmth of his hand. It came away in one piece, with the cork under it, with a small dry pop.
And something came out of the jar.
Juno saw it. Gold. A thin gold mist, like breath on a cold morning in the sun. It came up out of the neck of the jar, slow, and hung in the air, a little ball of light the size of an egg, just over the glass. Turning. Gently. As if it were looking round.
And Gideon leaned toward his father, and breathed.
Not hard. Not pushing. The way you breathe on a cold window. Slow and long and soft. Toward the big man's face. And the little ball of gold light moved on his breath, the way a feather moves, and drifted, and stretched out into a thin bright thread, and went across the small space between the boy's mouth and the man's face.
And as he breathed, Gideon said a word.
Very quietly. Flat. The way he said everything.
But not quite the way.
"Da."
